title: PodHood — WebMCP for Podcasts & YouTube
pitch: Turn any podcast or YouTube library into a surface your agent can drive: 8 WebMCP tools that search, filter, read timestamped transcripts, and cue the player on the page you're both looking at.
about_excerpt: Turn any podcast or YouTube library into a surface your agent can drive: 8 WebMCP tools that search, filter, read timestamped transcripts, and cue the player on the page you're both looking at. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into* Live demo → https://aiengineer.podhood.com * — a real production library of 1,065 talks. Open it in ChatGPT's in-app browser, or in Chrome with WebMCP enabled, and just start asking. Inspiration Podcasts and conference talks hold an enormous share of what a field actually knows, and almost none of it is reachable. Search gives you an episode, not a moment. A transcript is a 20,000-word wall. "Where did she explain the eval harness?" is a question no podcast page can answer today. Agents don't fix this — they inherit it. An agent that lands on a podcast page can do one of two unpleasant things: swallow the entire transcript and burn its context on filler, or drive the UI by guessing at pixels. Either way it works around the page instead of with it. WebMCP changes where the agent is standing. It is already here, in the browser, next to the person, looking at the same screen. That turns out to change what a tool is even allowed to be. What it does PodHood turns any podcast or YouTube channel into a structured library — summaries, chapters, key moments, speaker-diarized and word-aligned transcripts, recognized people, companies and products — and then registers that structure as eight WebMCP tools via document.modelContext , across two surfaces. On the library page search_episodes — search the catalog by meaning or keyword; returns episodes with timestamped citation links filter_episodes — apply topic / person / company / product / collection / year filters; the visible list and the URL change list_episodes — read back exactly what the visitor is looking at right now, with IDs open_episode — navigate the visitor to an episode page On an episode page read_episode — summary, speakers, and the chapter + key-moment outline with timestamps search_transcript — find exact text and highlight it in the transcript panel read_transcript — speaker-labeled, timestamped transcript windows, by chapter or time range play_moment — seek the player to a moment and start playback play_moment is the whole thesis in one call. The agent is not handing you a link to go read later. It moves the playhead in the player in front of you, and you hear the thing. That is only possible because the agent shares the view with a human — which is exactly the shape WebMCP has and no other agent interface does. What a human and an agent do together here On https://aiengineer.podhood.com — 1,065 talks from the AI Engineer conference series, 86 collections, 1,033 speakers, 880 companies — the loop looks like this: "What's actually being said about evals at these conferences?" → the agent runs search_episodes , then filter_episodes on the Evaluation & Observability topic. Your screen changes. You are now looking at 83 talks, and so is it. "Only 2026, and only speakers from model labs." → filter_episodes narrows again. You watch it happen, and you can undo it by clicking, because they are the same filters you would have clicked. "Open the second one and find where he explains the harness." → open_episode , then search_transcript . The line lights up in the transcript panel. "Play it." → play_moment . The player seeks and starts. You ask a follow-up while it plays; the agent has read_transcript scoped to that chapter and answers with a citation that points at your domain, at the right second. No copy-paste, no tab-switching, no "here's a link, go find it yourself." The agent does the navigating; the human does the listening and the deciding. Why WebMCP is the right primitive for this We already run a hosted MCP server for podcast catalogs, so we can compare the two honestly. An external MCP connector is a good way for an agent somewhere else to query a catalog. It cannot touch the page a person is looking at. It has no playhead, no transcript panel, no filter rail. WebMCP inverts that assumption, and the tools change shape as a result. filter_episodes is not a query — it is a UI mutation the person watches happen. search_transcript is not a string match — it is a highlight. This is the only agent interface where "tell me" and "show me" are the same call. Three properties we deliberately locked in: Read and view-state only. No writes, no accounts, no purchases. An agent can only change what the visitor could already change themselves — filters, highlight, playhead — all visible on screen and reversible with a click. There is no state an agent can reach that a human cannot see it reach. Show-branded, not platform-branded. The tools present as belonging to the creator's show, on the creator's domain — not to PodHood. Domain-native citations. Every link an agent produces resolves to the creator's own domain with a timestamp. Agent traffic lands on the creator, which is the only version of this that is sustainable for the people making the content. Why this needs more than a transcript Every tool here is downstream of structure that has to exist before the tool can be honest: search_episodes needs a semantic index over the catalog, not ctrl+F. filter_episodes needs entities disambiguated — "Claude" the model versus a person named Claude, three different speakers named Chen. play_moment needs word-level audio alignment . A timestamp four seconds off makes the entire feature feel broken. read_episode needs chapters and key moments that were actually extracted, not guessed at read time. This is the part of WebMCP we think is under-appreciated: good tools are a consequence of good data modeling. You can bolt document.modelContext onto anything. You can only make it useful on top of a page that already knows what it contains. How we built it The tool layer registers on document.modelContext when each surface mounts, with JSON-schema'd inputs and compact, agent-shaped return payloads — never raw DOM, never a whole transcript. Tools are bound to the same client state store the UI reads from , so an agent's filter_episodes and a human's click on the filter rail go down one code path. There is no drift between what the agent believes is on screen and what is on screen — and list_episodes exists precisely so the agent can re-ground itself against the real view at any point. read_transcript is windowed by chapter or time range, because handing a model ninety minutes of speech is how you get a confident wrong answer. Tool names and descriptions were tuned hard. A model will reach for search_episodes when it wants search_transcript unless the boundary is stated explicitly in the description. Next.js (App Router) + TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. Our origins are registered for the Chrome WebMCP origin trial, so document.modelContext is available with no flags — including on creators' custom domains. Zero creator configuration. The tools ship automatically with every published PodHood library. Nothing to enable, nothing to write. Agents without WebMCP support see a completely normal page; nothing degrades. Challenges we ran into Sizing outputs. The first read_transcript returned everything and the agent drowned. Chapter-scoped windows plus a "next window" affordance fixed it. One state, two drivers. Making agent-driven and human-driven state genuinely the same object took a refactor. Anything less produced ghost states, where the agent was filtering a list the human was not seeing. Restraint. The tempting move is to expose thirty tools. Eight sharply-described verbs outperformed a larger surface every time we tested. Testing against a moving target. WebMCP is an origin trial. ChatGPT desktop plus Chrome flags plus a live registered origin is not a fast dev loop. What we learned The best WebMCP tools are not an API bolted onto a page — they are the page's own verbs, named. Everything that worked here was already something the site could do: filter, highlight, seek. WebMCP just let an agent do it on the human's behalf, in front of them. The tools that tried to be more than the page could do were exactly the ones models misused. What's next Cross-library tools, so an agent can work across a creator's entire network of shows at once. A compare_moments tool for putting two speakers' claims side by side with both timestamps. Publishing the WebMCP tool layer as a standalone open-source package, so any media site can adopt the same eight verbs. Prior work vs. work done during the submission period PodHood is an existing product. The ingestion pipeline, the Brief data model (chapters, key moments, diarization, entity recognition, word-aligned transcripts), the search index and the player all predate this hackathon.
